title: The Spirit Who Gives Life (John 6:25–69)
transcript: Well, we have been hearing over the past few weeks that the Council of Nicaea was largely a refutation of Arius' teaching that the Son Jesus was created and had a beginning. And allegedly, sometimes this got quite physical. And the popular slogan of the day that was often shouted in the streets was this: 'en poti hotti uk'em.' And I thought this morning we might just be a rebellious crowd. We might try that together. Let's see how we can rebel and create a heresy. So let's do it. So we'll do it 3 times angrily, okay? So together, 'en poti hotti uk'em, en poti hotti uk'em, en poti un hotti uk'em.' You're not very rebellious at all. There was a time when he was not, is what that means. There was a time when he was not. And the opposition to his viewpoint, Arius' viewpoint, was led by Bishop Alexander and his protégé and the hero of our story thus far, Athanasius. And Athanasius insisted that the Spirit was eternally divine and had the same nature as the Father. As the Creed puts it, Jesus Christ, true God from true God. However, the unfortunate consequence of this protracted debate about the Son was that the status of the Holy Spirit was largely overlooked. The Creed of Nicaea in 325 simply says this: We believe in one God, the Father Almighty, and the Holy Spirit. And while that would make for a substantially shorter sermon, which many of you may regard as a blessing on this hot Sunday morning, it soon became clear that the church would need to define the relationship of the Father and the Son with the Spirit, without which, of course, our Christian faith would be binatarian and not Trinitarian. And the question was this: Was the Spirit simply the ministering angel sent to serve those who will inherit salvation that Hebrews 1 spoke of? Or was the Spirit part of the indivisible divine triad and therefore the same in worth and glory as the Father and the Son? Well, this question did not get resolved in Isaiah 3:2-5. Instead, the church fathers needed to gather a second time, this time in Constantinople, today's Istanbul, in 381. And there they would establish the relationship between the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit and find a form of words that were consistent with Scripture and affirmed the that the Spirit was fully God and co-equal with the Father and the Son. So this then is the modern version of that later extension of the Nicene Creed in 381: We believe in the Holy Spirit, the Lord, the giver of life, who proceeds from the Father, who with the Father and the Son is worshipped and glorified, who has spoken through the prophets. There is a lot of content contained within relatively few words there. So this morning I will mostly concentrate on the opening line, "I believe in the Holy Spirit, the Lord, the giver of life." Although my third point, I will touch on the other parts quite briefly. It is also worth saying now that this is not going to be a fully orbed presentation on the doctrine. Of the Holy Spirit. We will not consider the Spirit's gifts or his witness, his revelation, his baptism, personal indwelling, or the empowerment and mission of the church. At best, we'll touch on just one aspect of the Holy Spirit's work and so conclude something of the relationship to the Father and to the Son and subsequently to us. So let's take up our Bibles again, turn to that passage in John 6 if you would. And we take up the story immediately after the feeding of the 5,000, as Jenny had said. Jesus is on the shores of Lake Galilee and is being pursued by a large and demanding crowd and increasingly a suspicious Jewish leadership. And my first point this morning will be this: like father, like son. Our passage begins with what might be described as theological ping-pong, a match between Jesus and the crowd, an argument whose overall flow I would like us to follow this morning rather than to follow it line by line, as it were. Having fed the 5,000 on the shore of the Sea of Galilee, The disciples have now gotten into a boat, they have set off in the darkness, and they have crossed the lake for Capernaum, the green dot on the screen. On the morning, of course, the crowd wakes with the realization that Jesus is gone. And so they too get into their boats, they sail across the lake to find Jesus, and then confront him. And as they meet, Jesus' opening volley is to accuse them of chasing after him because they want him to satisfy their material needs, just as he had done yesterday, that they can again have their bellies filled. More than having any real interest in what Jesus' miraculous signs meant or said about him. So Jesus tells them plainly not to work for food that spoils but to work for food that endures to eternal life. They then ask him, "Well, What is this work that we are to do, this work that endures? To which Jesus replies, the work that's required of them is to believe, to believe, to believe in the one that God has sent to them. To which they respond, okay, if you want us to believe, 'Then you will need to give us a sign. After all, isn't that precisely what our ancestor Moses did to get the people to believe in him? He gave us manna. He gave us the bread from heaven.' Now clearly some form of mental amnesia has struck them since this scene immediately follows the feeding of the 5,000 where Jesus gave them bread from heaven. Precisely that. He'd give them a sign, bread from heaven. But clearly seeing is not always believing. So Jesus continues by correcting them, by pointing out that it was not Moses who gave you bread from heaven, but my Father who gives true bread from heaven. Notice the tense change here from "gave" to "gives," which is designed to make two points for us: that it was the Father who gave the bread, not Moses—that is, in the past—but also it is "my Father who now gives" in the present. And what he gives now is 'Is true bread, bread that will bring life to the world and not just for the Jews.' 'Okay,' they say, 'give us this bread.' To which Jesus replies, 'I am the bread. I am the bread of life.' For the first time, Jesus uses the 'I am' moniker to refere to himself in precisely the same way his Father had identified himself to Moses. If you recall the event in the Exodus story, Moses is standing before the Lord at the burning bush—who knew he was a good Presbyterian—and saying, "Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh and bring the Israelites out?" "Suppose I go to the Israelites and say to them, 'The God of your fathers has sent me to you,' and they ask me, 'What is his name?' What then shall I tell them?" So God said to Moses, "I am who I am. This is what you are to say to the Israelites: 'I am has sent me to you.'" Moses is to use God's personal covenantal name as his authority. Just as Moses gave manna to the people when they were hungry in the desert, so Jesus gave bread to the people who had gathered the day before. But now he presents himself as the better bread. Verse 49, have a look down at that. Your ancestors ate the manna in the wilderness, yet they died. But here is the bread that comes down from heaven, which anyone may eat and not die. I am the living bread that came down from heaven. Whoever eats this bread will live forever. 'Forever.' Lest you think the allusion to the Lord, to Yahweh, the 'I am,' is circumstantial, the crowd do not miss the implications of Jesus' words. They know exactly what Jesus is saying by taking the 'I am' saying to himself and by making the connection to Moses and manna in the desert. For immediately, we read, they start to grumble. And soon we are told this grumbling leads to going, as they abandon Jesus because of his claims. Why? Because Jesus is claiming God's identity and God's authority, and not for the first time. Chapter 6 continues what has already begun in the previous chapter about the authority of Jesus and the basis of his miraculous power. Two verses from there will help drive the main point home. Verse 21: For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, even so The Son gives life to whom he is pleased to give it. And verse 26: For as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son to have life in himself. Jesus is claiming prerogative powers, powers reserved for God himself. The power to give life. And why is that? Because like the Father, he too has life in himself. However, the point that John consistently makes in his Gospel is that people refuse to believe Jesus' claims, to believe in his claims. His words. In chapter 10, this is spelt out rather bluntly by Jesus, for there we read of the Jews coming to him and saying, 'If you are the Messiah, tell us plainly.' To which Jesus replies, 'I did tell you, but you do not believe. But the works I do in my Father's name testify about me.' The point Jesus is making there is this: that if you will not believe my words, then believe my works. I am who I say I am because of what I do. Just as the Father is able to give life, so I too can give life. Again, chapter 10 states this directly as Jesus tells the crowd, "I have come that they might have life and have it to the full." Jesus comes to earth so that you and I might have life. Better bread has been given by the Father. Not bread that perishes as the manna did, which rotted after 24 hours, but true bread. Bread that will sustain God's people into eternity. Bread that only God can give. The I Am kind of bread. Hence verse 57: The one who feeds on me will live. The life that Jesus offers to the world is precisely the same life that the Father brought to the world in creation. It's life that can arise out of nothing. Here is Jesus's claim to be God. Not created, not made, but true God from true God. And it was these kind of scriptural arguments that finally killed off the Arian arguments and settled the debates over the divinity of Jesus. And it helped the church fathers express the unity that exists between the Father and the Son, whereby Jesus could ultimately claim that "I and the Father are one," while still retaining the personal distinction between them. The Father is not the Son, and yet he is never without the Son. It is these claims that give rise to a Trinitarian theology that defines Christianity. Apart from the other Abrahamic faiths that we have today. And therefore I think these truths are well worth relearning. But what then of the Spirit? So point 2: like father, like son, like Holy Spirit. Arius has now been defeated, but later others such as the Tropici and then the Macedonians Macedonians arise to represent the same arguments, but this time against the full divinity of the Spirit. And thankfully, our hero Athanasius, he's still on the scene, and he writes 3 key letters to his friend Serapion to help him respond to these challenges. And the argument Athanasius uses is essentially the same as the one I have just presented, that the Holy Spirit must be God because he shares God's nature and does the things that only God can do. How do you recognize a firefighter?? Because they are the ones putting out the flames. And how do you recognise a doctor? Because they are the ones healing the sick. How do you recognise God? Because he is the one who gives life. He bestows it while creatures receive it. That's how Athanasius puts it. Only God has this power. In John 6, Jesus has just argued that he is the giver of life, the same giver as the Lord, the I Am, who revealed himself to Moses in the desert. And now Jesus turns to say exactly the same thing about the Spirit. Verse 63: The Spirit gives life. Gives life. The Spirit gives life. The flesh counts for nothing. The words that I spoke to you, they are full of spirit and life. Note the overlap here between what the Father gives, the Son gives, and now what the Spirit gives. All of them give life The argument that Jesus makes for himself can now equally be applied to the Spirit. Furthermore, the salvation that you and I enjoy, the eternal life promised to all who believe, is a result of the integrated work of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. All of them give life. But what then is the point of integration between them? How can all three persons be at work for our salvation without becoming competitors? Well, the answer is there in verse 40. For it is the Father's will that all 'Let everyone who looks on the Son and believes in him shall have eternal life.' Similarly, in verse 38, 'I have not come to do my will but the will of the Father.' It is the priority of the Father's will that coordinates the work of the Son and the Spirit. The Father redeems whom he will redeem. The Son accomplishes redemption and calls people to himself. And the Spirit applies redemption to the believer by initiating faith, uniting them to Christ, and sealing them for eternity. Therefore, as verse 37 puts it, all those the Father gives me will come to me. Or put negatively in verse 65, if you jump forward, "No one can come to me unless the Father has enabled them." Son and Holy Spirit are united in the Father's will and act to give eternal life to you and to me and to enable us to rest in that securely. Have a look, verse 39: "I shall lose none of those he has given me, but raise them up at the last day." Well then, thirdly, we need to return to the creed, for the various elements I have just mentioned concerning the Spirit are specifically identifiable within it. And I want to touch on three of those just very briefly before we close. And the first is to do with co-equal status. The status of the Spirit is divine and co-equal with the Father and the Son. And here the creed refers to the Spirit as the Lord, who with the Father and the Son is to be worshipped and glorified. We often think of the Lord of the Old Testament being associated with the Father and the God of Israel, a translation substitute, if you like, for Yahweh. Likewise, in the New Testament, it often refers to the Lord Jesus. But we are perhaps less familiar with the Spirit being identified as Lord. However, it is Paul who makes this lordship connection explicit for us as he writes to the Corinthians. "Now the Lord is the Spirit." The Lord is the Spirit. "And where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom." The implication is not only that the Spirit shares the same divine title as the Father and the Son, but that we also share in that obligation to receive and to obey the Spirit just as we would Jesus. It is fitting therefore that the Spirit receives equal honour and shares fully in the worship and glory of the Father and the Son. And secondly, the Word of God is Spirit-filled. Pamela said it earlier actually, that the Spirit in both Hebrew and Greek Greek can refer equally to the wind or even to breath. And it's this movement of the air that is understood as an essential aspect of our own ability to make the spoken word. John is playing on this idea to link both word and Spirit together. Jesus, the eternal Word, is the spoken Word who comes incarnate to be the living Word and who is recorded for us as the written Word. Hence the Creed's focus on the Spirit's prophetic Word who spoke to us through the prophets. The point being made is that the words of the prophets contain much more than mere information that point us to Jesus. Rather, they are life. They are Spirit-filled. As you listen now to Scripture being read, God is speaking life into you by his Spirit. Which then brings us thirdly to perhaps the most controversial point of the Nicene Creed, which is the language of double procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father, who proceeds from the Father and the Son. The addition of the 'and the Son' being affirmed actually much later at the Third Council of Toledo in 589. As the Father eternally begets the Son, so the equivalent language chosen for the Spirit was that he proceeds, or more simply put, goes forth from the Father. But it is the addition of the Son, the filioque clause as it's become known, that has proved much more controversial and divisive within the church. It's actually at the heart of the Great Schism that lies between the Church of the East and the Church of the West. And what has divided the church for a millennium will not be resolved by my closing remarks this morning. But as we have seen, both the Father and the Son cooperate in sending the Spirit as they do in all their actions. And that all three persons of the Trinity should be considered co-equal and share one divine being. And there is this clear association between the Word and the Spirit. And functionally, all three persons give life. So I will leave it to your personal conscience whether you understand that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son and the Son, or through the Son. But perhaps more importantly, we are finally brought to God's purpose for us, that we should be brought into communion with Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. As the disciples gathered in the upper room that first Easter, Jesus appeared among them, showed them his wounds, and wished them peace. And when he had done this, we read, he breathed on them and said to them, 'Receive the Holy Spirit.' Jesus gives his disciples, all those who have put their trust in him, the gift of the Holy Spirit. John Owen, the Puritan and English theologian, writes that the Spirit really, literally, and personally enters the believer, dwells within them, and grants them union with Christ. God's purpose is that we should live in communion with him. For he is within us. God is not some external agent but a person who makes their home within us. As believers then, we are brought into the Trinitarian life of God— Father, Son, and Holy Spirit And it is this reality that we affirm each time we say the creed together. Amen. Well, as the band comes up, let me end with part of John Stott's morning Trinitarian prayer. Let's pray. Heavenly Father, I pray that I may live this day in your presence and please you more and more. Lord Jesus, I pray that this day I might take up my cross and follow you. Holy Spirit, I pray that this day you will fill me with yourself and cause your fruit to ripen in my life. Love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control. Holy, blessed, and glorious Trinity, three persons in one God, have mercy upon me. Amen.
